issues.subcategory: p-value discrepancy between text and table
issues.description: The results text reports the sadness chi-square test as χ²(3)=8.74, p=.003, but Table 2 reports the same test with p=.033. For χ²(3)=8.74, the correct p-value is approximately .033 (matching the table). The p=.003 value in the text is incorrect by an order of magnitude. This misreported p-value affects the reader's evaluation of effect significance and cannot be attributed to rounding.
issues.quote: there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003

issues.subcategory: direction of iatrogenic effect misreported
issues.description: The text states that desire to die 'significantly decreased slightly' from pre (M=0.82) to post (M=1.03), but the means demonstrate an increase of +0.21 points, not a decrease. The table also confirms a change of +0.20. A statistically significant result (t(32)=2.23, p=.033) showing desire to die INCREASED after the study session is a clinically important iatrogenic finding that is being mischaracterized as a decrease. This has ethical implications for the reported safety profile of the procedure.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033

issues.subcategory: anxiety claimed significant in discussion but not in results
issues.description: The Discussion states that 'results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.' However, Table 2 shows that anxiety was not significant (χ²(3)=3.62, p=.306) in Analysis 1, and Table 3 shows anxiety was not significant in Analysis 2 (χ²(3)=2.31, p=.511). Anxiety never reached significance in any reported analysis. This mischaracterization inflates the apparent findings of the study.
issues.quote: results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness

issues.subcategory: episode duration inconsistency between methods and analysis
issues.description: The Methods section describes suicide attempt episodes as 'the one-week period prior to the attempt,' yet Analysis 2 uses a day variable 'ranging from -14 to 0,' indicating a 14-day (two-week) window. The Overview and Hypotheses section further states 'two weeks preceding a suicide attempt.' Other episode types are explicitly defined as two-week periods throughout. The discrepancy between the one-week description in episode identification and the two-week window in the analysis is never reconciled, raising questions about what data were actually analyzed.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a 'suicide attempt episode'

issues.subcategory: random effects structure dropped without specification
issues.description: For Analysis 2 (the primary interaction analysis), the paper states that models with the 'full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.' This means the final models for Analysis 2 contained only random intercepts, a dramatic departure from the maximal random effects structure recommended by Barr et al. (2013) and used for Analysis 1. Dropping random slopes can substantially inflate Type I error rates in mixed-effects models. The paper does not specify whether any partial random effects structure was attempted, what convergence criteria were used, or whether alternative optimizers were tried.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: beta sign direction inconsistent with stated effect for self-focus
issues.description: Table 3 reports negative beta coefficients for the self-focus interaction terms (β = -0.015 for Attempt vs. Ideation × Time; β = -0.010 for Attempt vs. Depressed × Time). If 'day' is coded from -14 to 0 (increasing toward attempt) and Attempt is the reference, negative betas would imply ideation and depressed show more increase than attempt over time, contradicting the stated finding that 'self-focus tended to increase preceding an attempt.' The sign and contrast coding is not sufficiently explained to allow readers to verify the stated direction of the effect.
issues.quote: self-focus tended to increase preceding an attempt, whereas depression and positive episodes were flatter and ideation appeared to show change over time in a downward direction

issues.subcategory: significant omnibus but no significant pairwise comparisons for death words
issues.description: The paper reports a significant interaction for death words (χ²(3)=9.47, p=.024) but then immediately notes that all pairwise comparisons are non-significant (zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739). Reporting a 'significant interaction' when no specific contrasts of theoretical interest are significant is misleading. Without multiple comparison correction and with no significant pairwise differences involving the attempt condition, this finding cannot support any substantive interpretation about suicide risk. The narration of this result as a meaningful 'significant interaction' inflates the apparent findings.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for death words, 2(3)=9.47, p=.024. However, there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes (zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739)

issues.subcategory: p-value typographical error
issues.description: The results report 'z=2.54, p=.0111' for the anger pairwise comparison between attempt and positive episodes. The value p=.0111 contains an extra digit and should presumably be p=.011. While likely a minor typographical error, it raises questions about the accuracy of other reported values and does not match the value in Table 3 (p=.011).
issues.quote: anger increased more steeply during attempt compared to all other episode types, including ideation (z=2.00, p=.046), depressed (z=2.49, p=.013), and positive (z=2.54, p=.0111) episodes

issues.subcategory: no pre-registration despite confirmatory hypotheses
issues.description: The paper presents specific, directional a priori hypotheses (greater self-focus, more negative sentiment, decreased social engagement prior to attempts) and tests them with inferential statistics. However, there is no mention of pre-registration. Without pre-registration, it is impossible to verify that the stated hypotheses were formulated before data collection and analysis, that the episode-type comparisons were planned, or that the decision to examine both mean and slope differences (Analysis 1 and Analysis 2) was pre-specified rather than chosen after observing the data.
issues.quote: In this study, we aimed to utilize ecological private SMS data to gain insight into possible novel, real-time digital biomarkers of suicidal behaviors.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc data-driven time window selection
issues.description: The paper states the two-week episode window was chosen 'in a conservative effort to capture the critical period' but then reveals it was also 'assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures' in which 'changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt.' Using the outcome data to inform the choice of temporal window constitutes a researcher degree of freedom that inflates Type I error. This data-driven window selection is not pre-specified and is not reflected in any correction to the subsequent inferential tests.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.subcategory: no multiple comparison correction across many tests
issues.description: The study runs a large number of statistical tests (at least 14 outcome variables × 2 analyses = 28 omnibus tests, plus multiple pairwise comparisons for each significant omnibus test) without any correction for familywise error rate. The authors explicitly justify this choice by citing Rothman (1990) and arguing the maximal random effects structure is 'overly conservative.' However, without correction, at alpha=.05, approximately 1-2 false positives are expected among the omnibus tests alone by chance. Several of the reported significant findings are borderline (e.g., anger p=.049, positive emotion vs. ideation p=.049), making the uncorrected approach particularly consequential.
issues.quote: we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction) but rather view any significant results in light of these caveats

issues.subcategory: undisclosed robustness analyses in supplement
issues.description: The paper mentions that 'additional analyses were performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results' and defers these to Supplement 3. The number, nature, and decision rules for these additional analyses are not described, creating undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom. It is unclear whether primary results were selected based on which analytic approach yielded significant results.
issues.quote: Additional analyses were performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results and to see if the pattern of results changed. Those analyses are available in Supplement 3 online.

issues.subcategory: majority of episodes lack SMS data with no differential analysis
issues.description: Of 293 total episodes collected across all participants, only 134 (46%) contained SMS data. The analyses are based exclusively on these 134 episodes. This 54% episode-level missingness is substantial and potentially non-random: episodes from further in the past are more likely to lack SMS data (older phones replaced, cloud backups unavailable), which means older attempts—potentially more severe or differently characterized—are systematically underrepresented. No comparison of episode characteristics with vs. without SMS data is reported.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.subcategory: excluded participants not characterized
issues.description: Six of 33 enrolled participants (18%) had no usable SMS data and were excluded from all primary analyses. No demographic or clinical comparison between included (n=27) and excluded (n=6) participants is reported. Given that exclusion was related to iPhone encryption settings and access to devices, the missing data mechanism is likely not missing at random (MNAR)—participants with more recent or higher-end iPhones with encryption may differ systematically from those without.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data.

issues.subcategory: retrospective episode identification introducing recall bias
issues.description: All episode boundaries (start and end dates) were determined through retrospective self-report during a laboratory interview. Participants retrospectively identified when they had suicidal crises, periods of ideation, depression, and positive mood—some potentially years in the past. This introduces well-documented retrospective biases: telescoping, boundary ambiguity, mood-congruent recall, and potential conflation of distinct episodes. The paper acknowledges only 90.3% of episodes were rated 'very' or 'somewhat' certain, meaning approximately 10% had dates the participants were uncertain about.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as 'very certain' (i.e., exact days) or 'somewhat certain' (i.e., may be off by a few days).

issues.subcategory: heterogeneous and low-lethality 'suicide attempt' definition
issues.description: The suicide attempt category includes actual enacted attempts, interrupted attempts (stopped by someone else), and aborted attempts (stopped by oneself) where 'no physical attempt was enacted.' The results confirm that 71% of incidents 'did not result in any physical harm.' This broad definition likely encompasses a very heterogeneous set of behaviors with substantially different levels of intent, planning, and lethality. Including aborted attempts where the person drove to a bridge but did not jump in the same category as someone who ingested a lethal dose of medication fundamentally compromises the construct validity of the high-risk episode type.
issues.quote: 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm (e.g., driving to high place, such as a bridge, but deciding not to jump)

issues.subcategory: study labeled 'prospective' despite retrospective design
issues.description: The paper claims to have 'utilized a prospective research design' by using retrospective recall to reconstruct timelines. This misapplies the term 'prospective.' The study design is retrospective: participants looked back to identify episodes, and data from those past periods were then extracted. While the SMS messages themselves were written in real time, the study design—in which the outcome (suicide attempt) is already known before the predictor (text message patterns) is analyzed—is retrospective and subject to biases the authors claim to have avoided.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: first-person pronoun use as rumination operationalization
issues.description: The study operationalizes self-focus/rumination using singular first-person pronouns ('I' words) from LIWC. First-person pronoun use is a grammatical feature driven by many factors unrelated to psychological self-focus (e.g., reporting events involving oneself, social context, gender norms in communication). LIWC's own documentation does not validate pronoun use as a rumination measure. The theoretical link from Baumeister's escape theory to pronoun frequency is tenuous—the theory describes cognitive deconstruction and emotional numbing as the escape mechanism, not necessarily linguistic self-reference.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: LIWC negation failure undermines sentiment construct validity
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that LIWC does not handle negation, meaning phrases like 'not happy' are counted as positive emotion words. This is a fundamental limitation for sentiment analysis. Since a substantial portion of emotional language in everyday texts likely includes negation (e.g., 'I'm not feeling great,' 'don't be sad'), the positive and negative emotion LIWC scores may systematically misclassify emotional content. This measurement error is non-trivial and could attenuate, inflate, or distort observed differences between episode types.
issues.quote: One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., 'not happy' would count as 'positive emotion' because negation is not accounted for)

issues.subcategory: sent/received message ratio as thwarted belongingness and burdensomeness
issues.description: The interpersonal theory of suicide specifies thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness as the key motivational constructs. The study operationalizes these as the ratio of sent vs. received text messages and word counts. This is an extremely distal behavioral proxy: message ratios are affected by conversational norms, phone plan, number of active relationships, work obligations, and many other factors unrelated to burdensomeness. The theoretical link between these constructs and raw message volume ratios is not validated.
issues.quote: we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages

issues.subcategory: use of proprietary non-transparent LIWC Tone variable
issues.description: The Emotional Tone variable from LIWC is described as a 'proprietary, non-transparent variable.' Including a measure whose computational basis is not disclosed makes it impossible for reviewers or replication researchers to understand what the construct captures, whether its properties are appropriate for this population and context, or how to interpret the reported effects. Using non-transparent proprietary measures violates open science principles and undermines replicability.
issues.quote: several proprietary, 'non-transparent' variables (e.g., Tone)

issues.subcategory: causal and predictive language used for retrospective correlational findings
issues.description: Throughout the paper, language implying causal prediction is used for what are correlational retrospective associations. Terms like 'digital biomarkers,' 'real-time digital markers of suicide risk,' 'identify suicide risk in real time,' and 'predict suicide attempt' imply that these linguistic patterns can be used prospectively to prevent suicide. The study design only establishes that SMS patterns differ (retrospectively identified) between episode types in a small, highly selected sample—a much weaker claim than real-time prediction.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: time-varying confounders not addressed in within-subjects design
issues.description: The within-subjects design controls for stable between-person confounders but does not control for episode-level time-varying confounders. Suicide attempt episodes likely co-occur with relationship crises, substance use, medication changes, financial stressors, or sleep disruption—all of which could independently affect language. Without measuring or controlling for these episode-specific factors, it is impossible to attribute observed language differences to suicide risk per se rather than to co-occurring contextual factors.
issues.quote: By comparing multiple periods of high vs. low suicide risk, all within a sample of suicide attempters, the current study attempted to trace how suicide risk changes dynamically

issues.subcategory: highly homogeneous WEIRD convenience sample with overclaimed generalizability
issues.description: The sample is 84.8% female, 60.6% White, mean age 20.4 years (SD=2.4), and 94% 'some college'—explicitly recruited from a university participant pool. The discussion and conclusion make broad claims about identifying suicide risk in the general population, developing clinical monitoring tools, and informing public health approaches. None of the reported results can generalize to males (who die by suicide at 4× the rate of females), older adults, non-college-educated populations, or non-White populations without substantial additional evidence.
issues.quote: Knowledge gained from this study could put us one step closer to the development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals' communication 'behind the scenes,' notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician or family if their patterns of communication indicate increasing levels of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: non-lethal attempter sample with overclaimed extrapolation to suicide completers
issues.description: By design, only individuals with non-lethal attempts could be studied. The paper acknowledges that 'characteristics of suicide attempters differ from those of suicide completers'—including higher burdensomeness in completers and a 4:1 male-to-female ratio for completions vs. attempts. Despite this, the abstract, introduction, and discussion frame the findings as informing tools to 'prevent future suicide-related behaviors' broadly, implicitly extending findings to completed suicide. The clinical utility of language markers specific to non-lethal attempts for preventing completed suicide is entirely undemonstrated.
issues.quote: While rates of attempt are greater for females, males are about four times more likely to die by suicide... It is possible that characteristics of suicide attempters differ from those of suicide completers

issues.subcategory: actual random effects structure for Analysis 2 never specified
issues.description: After stating that the maximal random effects model for Analysis 2 'did not converge' and that 'no random slopes were included in the final model,' the paper never specifies what random effects structure was actually estimated. It is unclear whether random intercepts for participant, participant-episode, and message were all retained or further simplified. Without this information, readers cannot evaluate the statistical model or replicate the analysis. This is particularly consequential because the significant findings (anger, positive emotion, self-focus interactions) all come from Analysis 2.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: no confidence intervals for any parameter estimates
issues.description: No confidence intervals are reported for any of the parameter estimates (β values, z-statistics, t-statistics). For a pilot study with acknowledged power limitations and multiple borderline p-values (e.g., p=.049, p=.046), confidence intervals are essential for evaluating the precision of estimates and the range of effect sizes consistent with the data. APA publication standards and open science guidelines recommend reporting confidence intervals for all parameter estimates.
issues.quote: β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes

issues.subcategory: power analysis uses inconsistent sample sizes
issues.description: The power analysis states the study has '30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect).' However, the study reports 27 participants with usable SMS data (not 20) and 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data (not from '60 attempts'). The discrepancy between the 20 in the power analysis and the 27 participants with SMS data, and the basis for the '60 attempts' figure, is unexplained. The power analysis appears to have been conducted using different assumed numbers than were actually observed.
issues.quote: a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes

issues.subcategory: distribution of messages across episode types not reported
issues.description: The paper reports 189,478 total text messages 'ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode' but does not report how messages were distributed across the four episode types. If attempt episodes systematically had fewer messages (e.g., because they were more temporally distant from data collection), this would create differential statistical power across episode comparisons and could confound results. The proportion of messages and episodes in each category is essential for evaluating the analyses.
issues.quote: Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode.

issues.subcategory: Baumeister escape theory misapplied to predict increased self-focus
issues.description: The paper invokes Baumeister's (1990) escape from self theory to predict greater first-person pronoun use prior to suicide attempts. However, Baumeister's theory predicts that unbearable self-awareness leads to cognitive deconstruction—a state of reduced meaningful self-reflection, emotional numbing, and concrete thinking—as the escape mechanism. The theory does not straightforwardly predict increased linguistic self-reference during the pre-attempt period; it may instead predict decreased self-focused language as cognitive deconstruction sets in. The authors' directional prediction of increased self-focus is not the most direct derivation from the cited theory.
issues.quote: one theory of suicide posits that suicide is a means to escape from negative self-focus (Baumeister, 1990). It follows that the feedback loop of increasing self-focus and painful recognition of self-failures may lead someone to act on their suicidal thoughts

issues.subcategory: term 'digital biomarker' misapplied to behavioral linguistic patterns
issues.description: The paper repeatedly uses the term 'digital biomarkers' to describe linguistic patterns in text messages. The biomarker terminology in medicine and psychiatry refers to measurable biological indicators (physiological, biochemical, or molecular signals). Applying this term to behavioral/linguistic outputs from text messages inappropriately borrows the precision and clinical authority of biological measurement. This conceptual overreach may mislead readers about the nature and reliability of the evidence, and misrepresents where this work sits in the prediction-to-clinical-implementation pipeline.
issues.quote: we aimed to utilize ecological private SMS data to gain insight into possible novel, real-time digital biomarkers of suicidal behaviors

issues.subcategory: post-hoc activation explanation for attempt-positive mood similarity in self-focus
issues.description: When self-focus failed to differentiate attempt from positive mood episodes, the authors propose post-hoc that both involve heightened 'energy and activation,' which explains the similarity. This explanation contradicts the theoretical premise that self-focus maps linearly onto suicide risk. No prior theory predicts that positive mood and suicide attempt episodes should show similar self-focus trajectories due to shared activation. This is a classic case of post-hoc theorizing that immunizes null results against falsification and is presented without empirical support.
issues.quote: it is plausible that there are similarities between psychological states during attempt and during positive episodes, which may be reflected by similarities in language use... self-focus may be especially sensitive to changes in risk related to increased energy or activation

issues.subcategory: abstract null result claim contradicted by discussion positive claims
issues.description: The abstract states 'no language features uniquely differentiated suicide attempts from other episodes' for mean differences, which is accurate. However, the Discussion states 'results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.' Sadness was only significantly higher than ideation (not depressed or positive), and anxiety was never significant. This asymmetry between accurate abstract reporting and inflated discussion claims creates misleading impressions of the findings for readers who read only one section.
issues.quote: Regarding mean differences, no language features uniquely differentiated suicide attempts from other episodes.

issues.subcategory: episode type classification based on participant subjective interpretation
issues.description: Episode classification into attempt, ideation, depressed, or positive categories was based substantially on participants' own interpretations of their past behaviors. The paper acknowledges this explicitly, noting that some 'suicide attempts' were endorsed because participants 'subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions' even when 'no physical attempt was enacted.' This creates a circularity: the independent variable (episode type) is based on participants' subjective self-classification using the same screener questions that defined their study inclusion, without independent clinical verification of episode type.
issues.quote: reported 'suicide attempts' also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than 'suicide ideation' so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions
